Your device has dropped from a newer radio technology (4G/5G) to an older one (2G/3G) while standing still, with no voice call in progress. IMSI catchers force this because the older protocols have weaker encryption and are easier to intercept. Legitimate networks only downgrade where there is no newer coverage, and a phone without VoLTE drops to 3G or 2G for every call; Clairix does not count a reading taken during a call or within five minutes of one.

Avoid making voice calls or sending SMS until you leave the area. Use end-to-end encrypted messaging apps over WiFi or data. Do not transmit sensitive information. Move away from the area and observe whether the technology level returns to normal. %1$s

High confidence indicator. A drop to 2G/3G within half an hour of 4G/5G serving you at the same spot, without you having moved and without a call, is a primary IMSI catcher signature. Moving resets the comparison, so a drive into a basement car park does not count, and neither does a call falling back to the older network.

A cell tower ID that you have seen before, on the same radio technology, is now claiming to be in a different area (tracking area code). Real base stations have fixed area assignments. A portable IMSI catcher borrowing a real cell\'s number produces inconsistent area codes.
Monitor for additional indicators. A single mismatch could be a network reconfiguration, but combined with other findings it is significant. Avoid sensitive calls in this area.

High confidence indicator when combined with other findings. Alone it may reflect a carrier re-plan: if this cell keeps reporting the new area consistently for forty readings over an hour or more, Clairix accepts the new area as its baseline and this finding clears.

Your device registered a different tracking area while you were not moving. Tracking area changes normally happen when you travel across cell boundaries. When you are stationary, a change indicates a new transmitter has appeared near you and forced re-registration.
Note your exact location and time. A stationary area change combined with other indicators is a strong surveillance signal. Consider moving away from the area.

Medium confidence. Stationary area changes can occur due to legitimate network maintenance, but are uncommon and warrant attention alongside other findings. A change during a voice call, or within five minutes of one, is not counted: a call can move the phone to another network layer.

The cell signal is significantly stronger than the historical maximum for this area. A portable transmitter placed near you — in a vehicle, building, or backpack — produces a much stronger signal than a distant tower.

Check your surroundings for parked vehicles with unusual equipment, people lingering nearby, or recently placed objects. A strong signal alone is insufficient for action, but note the location and observe whether it moves with you.
Medium confidence. Signal strength varies for many reasons. This indicator is most meaningful when combined with technology downgrade or unknown cell findings.

A cell tower that has never appeared in this area before has become your serving cell. You have visited this area at least 20 separate times, and the tower infrastructure here is well-established. Portable IMSI catchers appear as unknown cells in familiar areas.

A new cell at a familiar location deserves caution. If you also see technology downgrade or signal strength anomalies, treat this as a serious surveillance indicator. Do not make sensitive calls. Move away and observe whether the new cell disappears.
Medium confidence. New towers do get installed occasionally, but this detection requires at least 20 separate visits to the area (returns more than 30 minutes apart) before triggering.

A cell tower appeared briefly as your serving cell, then vanished. Real base stations broadcast continuously — they do not appear for a few minutes and disappear. A portable surveillance device driven into and away from an area looks exactly like this.
Note the time and location. An ephemeral cell that appeared and disappeared suggests a mobile surveillance asset that has moved on. Review your surroundings at the time of detection.

Medium-to-high confidence. Ephemeral cells have few legitimate explanations once the two common ones are ruled out: a cell that served while you were moving, and a 3G or 2G cell that carried a voice call on a phone without VoLTE, are never counted. A duration under 90 seconds is the strictest threshold.

Your device has switched between multiple different cell towers rapidly while you were stationary. IMSI catchers force repeated re-registrations to capture authentication events. Normal network handover does not produce this pattern at a single location.
Avoid making calls or sending messages while this is occurring. If it persists, move away from the area. The flapping pattern suggests active interference with your device\'s network registration.
Medium confidence. Rapid cell switching can also result from poor coverage areas, but is unusual when stationary in a normally covered location.

Your serving cell is reporting zero neighbouring cells. Real base stations always have overlapping coverage with adjacent towers — this is fundamental to how cellular networks are designed. A portable IMSI catcher operating alone has no neighbours to report.

This is a supporting indicator rather than an action trigger alone. Watch for it alongside technology downgrade or unknown cell findings, at which point you should follow the high-confidence response guidance.
Low confidence as a standalone indicator. Meaningful when combined with other findings.

LTE timing advance of zero means the transmitter serving you is within about 78 metres. A rooftop site, an in-building antenna or a small cell is this close legitimately, and so is a portable IMSI catcher in a parked vehicle or a nearby building. On its own the reading does not say which.

Nothing on its own. If it appears together with other indicators, note the time and place, look for a vehicle or equipment that was not there before, avoid sensitive calls and see whether the indicator follows you when you move.

Low confidence alone. The distance is a precise physical measurement; what is at that distance is not. Clairix remembers each cell: once one has read timing advance zero on twenty readings spread over a day, it treats that as normal there and stops listing it.

The signal strength on your current cell tower jumped suddenly between two consecutive readings. A macro cell tower at a fixed location has a stable signal. A mobile transmitter moving towards you — in a vehicle, for example — produces exactly this kind of spike.

A sudden signal spike suggests a mobile surveillance asset moving closer to your position. Be aware of your surroundings. If the spike is combined with other indicators, follow the high-confidence response protocol immediately.
Medium confidence. Signal spikes can result from device movements, building reflections, or other environmental factors, but are notable when combined with other findings.

Your device has switched between three or more radio technologies (2G, 3G, 4G, 5G) in a short window while standing still and not on a call. IMSI catchers force devices through technology cycles to capture separate authentication events on each technology, revealing the device\'s IMSI. A voice call on a phone without VoLTE walks 5G to 3G and back on its own, so readings taken in a call, or within five minutes of one, are not counted.

Multiple technology switches in a short window strongly indicate active interference. Avoid all calls and data use. Use WiFi with a VPN for any communications. Move out of the area and observe whether the switching stops. %1$s
High confidence. Rapid multi-technology oscillation outside a call is a strong signature of active IMSI capture operations.
An anomaly was detected in your cellular environment that deviates from your established baseline. The specific indicator ID is: %1$s. See the full detail for more context.

What a sensor by the road gets

A Bluetooth receiver on a pole, in a shop or in a patrol car logs every address it hears, with the time. It cannot open the phone or read anything off it. The phone itself advertises on an address Android changes every quarter of an hour, so it is hard to follow; your accessories are not. A car\'s hands-free, most earbuds and many watches keep one address for life, and it is logged at every sensor they pass. Flock\'s plate readers themselves do not listen for Bluetooth; separate sensors do, and the two kinds of record are easy to join.

Where Wi-Fi and cell towers put you

The satellites and the Wi-Fi and cell position put this phone in different places. A spoofer moves the satellite position; a mis-mapped access point or a stale cell fix moves the other. Clairix cannot tell which is wrong, so do not navigate by either until they agree again.
The checks run while this screen is open. Start the scanner to keep them running in the background whenever the GPS is on, as it is when you navigate.
What this can and cannot catch

It catches the spoofers that are cheap to build: one transmitter on the ground, a recording replayed, a simulator started at the wrong time, a mock-location app. A careful attacker who simulates a full sky at realistic strengths and the right time passes the signal tests; the Wi-Fi and cell comparison is the one they cannot pass while a tower or access point is in range. That comparison needs a Wi-Fi/cell position source on the phone and the cross-check on (Settings, Location); its row says when it cannot run. Not every phone reports raw measurements or gain, and those checks say so instead of passing.

Every comms connection, not only this check, is held to the pinned key: a different one is refused even when the phone\'s trust store accepts it, which is what a coerced certificate authority would produce. Comms then stop until you forget the pin here. Expect that once whenever the relay\'s certificate is renewed with a new key.

Someone who knows you rarely needs an app to watch you. A Google or Samsung account they also sign in to, location sharing, a family group, a recovery number they control or calls forwarded at the carrier show them as much, and no app on the phone can see any of it, Clairix included. • Every conversation, contact, group and call record, and the keys behind them

• Every notification and Clairix's notification categories, the clipboard, the push registration and the device-admin role

In this order: every key in the phone\'s secure hardware, then every file, setting and database; then the relay is asked, for a few seconds, to delete the account, and Clairix closes. It opens next as a new install. There is no undo and no backup to restore from.

If the relay cannot be reached, the request to delete the account waits on this phone, in a file that holds your Clairix number, the relay\'s address and copies of the request signed with your identity key, and is tried again about every ten minutes, whether or not Clairix is open, for up to a day; after that, write to support@clairix.app. Uninstalling Clairix deletes that file, so a request still waiting then is never sent. With Tor on, it is sent only through Tor, before Clairix closes, and is not kept or tried again.

Android keeps what is its own: Clairix stays installed, and Settings still lists the access you gave it, its battery and location use, and how many notification categories it has deleted. When having the app at all is the risk, uninstall it afterwards.

The wrong-passcode limit runs the same wipe. So does the duress passcode at the lock screen, with one difference: Clairix does not close. It stays on its lock screen, and from then on that code opens it, empty.
